title: Post-pandemic social connection was broadly stable in Belgium, but young people and those living alone show specific functional losses
source_unit: Verhaegen et al., Social connection before and after the COVID-19 pandemic: results of the Belgian Health Interview Survey, BMC Public Health 2026
geography: Belgium, national population aged 15 years and older, with stratified analyses by age, household situation, sex, and education

denominator.unit: Belgian Health Interview Survey participants: 2018 N=8075 and 2023-2024 N=4926, age 15+

general_change.value: no statistically significant pre/post difference in social-contact frequency, social support, or social satisfaction in the general population

structural_connection.value: social-contact frequency showed no significant difference between 2018 and 2023-2024

functional_connection.value: social support and social satisfaction showed no general pre/post difference, although finer response distributions suggest a subtle shift from very satisfied toward rather satisfied

recovery_interpretation.value: by 2023-2024, broad Belgian social connection appears more recovered or stable than a simple permanent-decline narrative would imply

observations.method: National household health surveys using registry-based multi-stage stratified sampling, post-stratification weighting, and logistic regression comparing 2018 with 2023-2024.
observations.uncertainty: The study is repeated cross-sectional rather than longitudinal, lacks an acute-pandemic measurement, and measures selected structural and functional components rather than qualitative relationship quality, loneliness in a fully comparable way, or within-person change.
observations.subgroup: Belgian residents aged 15 years and older, with population-level estimates of contact frequency, perceived social support, and social satisfaction.
observations.counterinterpretation: A stable national average can conceal localized or subgroup harms, measurement insensitivity, changes in relationship quality, or social changes not captured by the selected indicators.

observations.period: 2018 versus 2023-2024; adolescents and young adults aged 15-24

denominator.unit: stratified age-group comparison within the Belgian Health Interview Survey

poor_social_support.value: 15-24-year-olds had higher odds of poor social support after the pandemic than before it

other_indicators.value: the study found no significant age-group pre/post effect for social-contact frequency or social satisfaction among 15-24-year-olds

developmental_route.value: the authors identify youth social support as a specific point of concern because adolescence and young adulthood depend heavily on close social development and peer connection

observations.method: Stratified logistic-regression analysis of the repeated national health surveys, with age-group interaction and subgroup comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The result is an indication from repeated cross-sectional data, not proof that pandemic policies caused the change; small subgroup combinations require caution and the study does not identify the role of school, work, telework, digital media, or household transitions.
observations.subgroup: Belgian adolescents and young adults aged 15-24.
observations.counterinterpretation: The shift may reflect cohort, economic, educational, or broader generational changes unrelated to the pandemic, and poor social support may not imply reduced contact frequency or dissatisfaction.

denominator.unit: stratified household-situation comparison within the Belgian Health Interview Survey

social_satisfaction.value: people living alone had higher odds of low social satisfaction after the pandemic than before it

baseline_inequality.value: people living alone also had poorer social connection in general than those not living alone

outside_household_dependence.value: living alone increases reliance on contacts outside the household for social needs, making disruptions to out-of-household connection especially consequential

younger_intersection.value: the post-pandemic social-satisfaction difference was particularly pronounced among younger people living alone

observations.method: Stratified and interaction analyses of nationally sampled Belgian health-survey data, using social satisfaction and household situation measures.
observations.uncertainty: The cross-sectional design cannot establish within-person decline or causality; living alone may proxy age, housing affordability, relationship status, migration, work, health, or other conditions not fully separated in the comparison.
observations.subgroup: Belgian residents living alone, especially younger people living alone.
observations.counterinterpretation: Living alone does not necessarily mean social isolation, and low satisfaction may reflect changing expectations, relationship quality, or housing and labor conditions rather than pandemic effects alone.

denominator.unit: repeated Belgian Health Interview Survey time series since 1997 for available indicators

infrequent_contacts.value: the percentage reporting infrequent social contacts increased over the long run but appeared to stabilize in the most recent waves

low_social_satisfaction.value: low social satisfaction showed a significant increasing long-run trend since the start of measurement

inequality_route.value: social connection is patterned by living alone and education even when national post-pandemic averages are stable

policy_implication.value: preparedness and social policy should target vulnerable life situations rather than assume a uniform national recovery or decline

observations.method: Descriptive contextualization of repeated national survey indicators alongside the 2018 versus 2023-2024 comparison.
observations.uncertainty: Available time-series indicators use different questions and may not capture qualitative relationship quality, changing norms, or all dimensions of loneliness and connection.
observations.subgroup: Belgian population, with attention to people living alone, youth, education groups, and other sociodemographic strata.
observations.counterinterpretation: Long-run trends may reflect reporting changes, demographic shifts, household composition, and survey instruments as well as genuine changes in social life.

related_sources.claim: Open-access BMC Public Health article with abstract, methods, results, subgroup findings, limitations, and long-run context.
Publisher PDF for the 12-page peer-reviewed article.

boundary: This record adds a comparative social-connection route from pandemic-era disruption through national recovery, youth support, living alone, education, social satisfaction, and policy targeting. It is nationally sampled repeated cross-sectional evidence from Belgium, not a longitudinal causal estimate, global trend, qualitative relationship assessment, or proof that pandemic policy caused subgroup changes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Publisher article and accessible full-text source reviewed for survey waves, sample sizes, social-connection dimensions, national findings, youth and living-alone subgroup results, long-run context, methods, and limitations.
